input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-635: Introduction to Machine Learning. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: This course offers an introduction to supervised machine learning theories and algorithms, and their application to classification and regression tasks. Topics include: Mathematical background of machine learning (e.g. statistical analysis and visualization of data), neural models (e.g. Convolutional Neural Networks, Recurrent Neural Networks), probabilistic graphical models (e.g. Bayesian networks, Markov models), and reinforcement learning. Programming assignments are required. Prerequisites: (CSCI-603 or CSCI-605 with a grade of B or better) or ((CSCI-243 or SWEN 262) and (MATH-251 or STAT-205)) or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

Source excerpts:

[nist-ai-rmf]
The NIST AI Risk Management Framework organizes work around Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. Govern establishes policies, responsibilities, and accountability for AI risk. Map documents context, intended use, affected people, and potential impacts. Measure uses qualitative and quantitative methods to analyze identified risks. Manage prioritizes risks and allocates resources for response and monitoring. Risk analysis considers data quality and uncertainty. It also considers robustness, privacy, security, transparency, and fairness. Monitoring continues after deployment because context and system behavior can change.

[rit-csci-635]
This course offers an introduction to supervised machine learning theories and algorithms, and their application to classification and regression tasks. Topics include: Mathematical background of machine learning (e.g. statistical analysis and visualization of data), neural models (e.g. Convolutional Neural Networks, Recurrent Neural Networks), probabilistic graphical models (e.g. Bayesian networks, Markov models), and reinforcement learning. Programming assignments are required. Prerequisites: (CSCI-603 or CSCI-605 with a grade of B or better) or ((CSCI-243 or SWEN 262) and (MATH-251 or STAT-205)) or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

[scikit-learn-user-guide]
Machine-learning workflows separate data preparation, training, validation, testing, model selection, and evaluation. Supervised methods learn a mapping from examples paired with target labels. Unsupervised methods identify structure without target labels. Preprocessing must be fitted only on permitted training data to avoid leakage. Pipelines combine preprocessing and estimators so the same transformations are applied consistently. Cross-validation repeats training and validation across defined data splits. Evaluation metrics must match the task and the cost of different errors. Hyperparameter selection must remain separate from final test evaluation. Leakage, distribution shift, overfitting, and unexamined assumptions can invalidate results.

beats.claim: CSCI-635 introduces supervised machine learning theories and algorithms for classification and regression tasks, with required programming assignments.
beats.example: Students will implement a basic classification model using scikit-learn to predict customer churn from tabular data.
beats.title: Course Foundations and Scope
beats.visualDirection: Display a slide showing the course title, duration (8-12 min), and a simple flowchart linking 'Supervised Learning' to 'Classification/Regression' with a note about programming assignments.

beats.claim: The mathematical background of machine learning includes statistical analysis and visualization of data to understand distributions and relationships.
beats.example: Students will plot a histogram and scatter plot of training data to identify outliers and feature correlations before model training.
beats.title: Mathematical Background and Data Visualization
beats.visualDirection: Show a split-screen image: left side shows a histogram of a continuous feature, right side shows a scatter plot of two features, with axes labeled and a legend indicating 'Training Data Distribution'.

beats.claim: Machine-learning workflows separate data preparation, training, validation, testing, model selection, and evaluation to ensure reproducible results.
beats.example: Students will use a scikit-learn Pipeline to standardize features and train a logistic regression model without mixing preprocessing steps across splits.
beats.title: Machine Learning Workflows and Data Preparation
beats.visualDirection: Display a horizontal timeline graphic with six labeled nodes: 'Data Preparation', 'Training', 'Validation', 'Testing', 'Model Selection', 'Evaluation', connected by arrows indicating sequential execution.

beats.claim: Preprocessing must be fitted only on permitted training data to avoid leakage, and cross-validation repeats training and validation across defined data splits to assess generaliz.
beats.example: Students will implement StratifiedKFold cross-validation to evaluate a random forest classifier, ensuring scaling is applied only within each fold's training set.
beats.title: Preventing Data Leakage and Cross-Validation
beats.visualDirection: Show a diagram of a dataset split into 5 folds, with one fold highlighted as 'Validation' and the others as 'Training', accompanied by a warning icon labeled 'No Leakage'.

beats.claim: Evaluation metrics must match the task and the cost of different errors to accurately assess model performance and guide improvement decisions.
beats.example: Students will compare precision, recall, and F1-score for a medical diagnosis classifier, weighting recall higher due to the high cost of false negatives.
beats.title: Evaluation Metrics and Error Costs
beats.visualDirection: Display a comparison table with columns for 'Metric', 'Definition', and 'Use Case', highlighting 'Recall' under 'High Cost of False Negatives' with a red alert icon.

beats.claim: Neural models such as Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent Neural Networks are applied to structured data like images and sequences, respectively.
beats.example: Students will train a CNN on a dataset of handwritten digits to classify images, and an RNN on a time-series dataset to predict stock prices.
beats.title: Neural Models: CNNs and RNNs
beats.visualDirection: Show two side-by-side architecture diagrams: left shows a CNN with convolutional and pooling layers processing an image, right shows an RNN with hidden states processing a sequence of data points.

beats.claim: Probabilistic graphical models like Bayesian networks and Markov models represent complex dependencies and uncertainties through directed or undirected graphs.
beats.example: Students will construct a Bayesian network to model the probability of disease given symptoms, using conditional probability tables for each node.
beats.title: Probabilistic Graphical Models
beats.visualDirection: Display a directed acyclic graph with nodes labeled 'Symptom A', 'Symptom B', and 'Disease', connected by arrows indicating causal relationships, with probability values annotated on edges.

beats.claim: Reinforcement learning involves agents learning optimal policies through trial and error, receiving rewards or penalties for actions in dynamic environments.
beats.example: Students will train an agent to navigate a grid environment using Q-learning, adjusting actions based on cumulative reward signals.
beats.title: Reinforcement Learning Basics
beats.visualDirection: Show a simple grid environment with an agent icon, arrows indicating possible actions, and a reward value (+1 or -1) displayed at each step, with a 'Policy' label indicating the learned strategy.

beats.claim: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework organizes work around Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage to address risks like data quality, robustness, privacy, security, transparency, and.
beats.example: Students will document a risk map for a deployed recommendation system, identifying potential biases in training data and outlining monitoring procedures for post-deployment performance.
beats.title: NIST AI Risk Management Framework
beats.visualDirection: Display a four-quadrant diagram labeled 'Govern', 'Map', 'Measure', 'Manage', with each quadrant containing a brief description and a relevant icon (e.g., shield for security, magnifying glass for measurement).

beats.claim: A practical analysis checklist ensures that data quality, distribution shift, overfitting, and unexamined assumptions are evaluated before deploying machine learning models.
beats.example: Students will complete a checklist verifying that preprocessing was fitted only on training data, cross-validation was used, evaluation metrics matched the task, and monitoring plans are in place.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Show a clean checklist graphic with six items: 'Data Quality Verified', 'No Leakage Detected', 'Metrics Match Task', 'Cross-Validation Applied', 'Distribution Shift Assessed', 'Monitoring Plan Established', with checkboxes and a 'Pass/Fail'

learningObjectives: Define supervised machine learning workflows and explain how to prevent data leakage through proper preprocessing and cross-validation.
Explain the core components of machine learning evaluation metrics and their relationship to task-specific error costs.
Describe the NIST AI Risk Management Framework's four pillars and how they apply to machine learning deployment and monitoring.
